reference.source: Respiratory Medicine reference texts and pneumotox literature
clinicalPearls: A diagnosis of exclusion requiring a temporal link between a culprit drug and new interstitial lung disease, with improvement after withdrawal supporting causation
Classic offenders include amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, bleomycin and other chemotherapy agents, and increasingly immune checkpoint inhibitors and molecular targeted therapies

Radiological and histological patterns vary widely, encompassing organising pneumonia, non-specific interstitial pneumonia, hypersensitivity-like pneumonitis, diffuse alveolar damage, and eosinophilic pneumonia
Amiodarone toxicity is suggested by high-attenuation liver and lung deposits on CT reflecting the iodinated drug
Nitrofurantoin can cause both an acute hypersensitivity reaction and a chronic fibrosing pneumonitis with long-term use
Checkpoint-inhibitor pneumonitis is an immune-related adverse event that can be rapidly progressive and may require drug cessation and immunosuppression
A thorough medication history, including over-the-counter drugs, recent chemotherapy, and radiotherapy, is essential
reference.pathophysiology: Drugs injure the lung through several mechanisms: direct cytotoxicity to alveolar epithelial and endothelial cells (as with cytotoxic chemotherapy), oxidant-mediated damage, phospholipid accumulation (as with amiodarone), and immune or hypersensitivity reactions in which the drug or its metabolites trigger an inflammatory response. The resulting injury manifests as varied histological patterns depending on the agent, dose, and host susceptibility, ranging from reversible inflammatory pneumonitis and organising pneumonia to diffuse alveolar damage and established fibrosis. Immune checkpoint inhibitors act differently, unleashing T-cell-mediated inflammation of the lung as an autoimmune-like adverse event. Recognition of the offending drug and its withdrawal are central, as continued exposure risks progression to irreversible fibrosis.
additionalDifferentials: Infection, including opportunistic pneumonia in immunosuppressed patients
Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease
Progression or lymphangitic spread of underlying malignancy
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution CT to define the pattern and distribution of disease
Comprehensive drug and treatment history cross-referenced against known pulmonary toxins
Bronchoalveolar lavage to characterise cellularity and exclude infection
Pulmonary function tests with diffusing capacity
Lung biopsy in selected cases where diagnosis remains uncertain
Exclusion of infection with microbiological and serological testing
Monitoring of response after withdrawal of the suspected agent
redFlags: Rapidly progressive hypoxaemia suggesting diffuse alveolar damage or severe checkpoint-inhibitor pneumonitis
Continued administration of a suspected culprit drug despite deterioration
Concurrent features of infection that could be masked or worsened by immunosuppression
reference.prognosis: Many inflammatory patterns improve after drug withdrawal, with or without corticosteroids for drug-induced ILD, but agents causing diffuse alveolar damage or established fibrosis, and severe checkpoint-inhibitor pneumonitis, carry a substantial risk of persistent impairment or death.
pitfalls: Failing to obtain a complete drug history and missing the causative agent
Attributing all new infiltrates to infection or malignancy progression in oncology patients
Continuing the offending drug because the diagnosis was not considered
Overlooking that some agents (e.g. nitrofurantoin) cause both acute and chronic forms
